Bart Willemsen is developing eight films and series. One of them, Kachhua, is in funded development with a London co-producer and a BAFTA-winning writer. None of it is visible anywhere. This is what it looks like when it is.

Warana develops and produces character-driven films and series with international ambition. The world a story happens in matters as much as the person it happens to.

In October 2015 a lawyer named Afroz Shah began clearing Versova Beach in Mumbai, with only his 84-year-old neighbour to help. He came back one hundred weeks in a row. More than 4,000 tonnes of waste have been removed from two and a half kilometres of sand. The United Nations called it the largest beach clean-up in the world.
A boy fights his way out of the poverty of a Mumbai slum. Success brings the understanding that he can only go on if he returns to face the shadows of a past that keeps catching up with him.

Afroz Shah grows up beside Versova Beach, between a loving mother and a troubled father. As a child he watches hatchling turtles crawl to the sea there, with his father beside him. Years later he is a successful lawyer, but the past has not let go of him. He returns to the beach of his childhood and finds it buried under waste — a place no turtle could safely come back to. He starts clearing it alone. What follows grows into a movement of thousands of people.
When her beloved beagle puppy is sold to the daughter of a celebrity chef, a farmer's daughter named Bente befriends her to get him back.
After her mother dies, 22-year-old photographer Isa travels to Cape Town to get answers from the father who left her years ago.

In the slate every project gets its own colour wash over the image. That is not an accident, and it works: you can tell the eight titles apart without adding a single logo. This is a project palette. Use it everywhere — on the site, in the feed, on every document that belongs to a title.

The slate pairs the logo with a serif and a sans that both sit close to whatever a design tool hands you by default. They are not wrong; they are unowned — you have seen them on a hundred other decks. The wordmark WARANA is a Didone: high contrast, thin hairlines, real character. Give it a display face that answers it instead of blending in.
• Keep clear space around the logo, at least the height of the arc on every side.
• Leave the documentary photographs from India unfiltered. Those are the only real images you have, and they are worth more than all the renders put together.
• Put the logo on a busy image without darkening what sits behind it. The hairline of the arc vanishes.

What I am looking for is not one big cheque. Across eight titles we are talking about roughly twenty million, and that never comes from one place. It comes from funds, from rebates in three countries, from co-producers who bring their own national support, from pre-sales — and from a slice somebody has to be willing to carry.
Right now I am looking for three things: a co-producer for the Red Sea title, a Dutch distributor for the family films, and conversations with investors who understand that development takes years.

The Dutch Production Incentive pays out a maximum of €3 million per year per production company. That one rule decides the shape of everything that follows. Below: eight sources, what each one actually is, and what has to be on the table before you knock.
SunnyMarch in the UK and A Team Productions in Belgium each bring their own national support.
The final gap, covered against unsold territories.
A fully costed budget per title, a demonstrable share of the financing already in place, and a production schedule that fits inside the rounds.
Development and production grants, applied for title by title in the regular rounds. For a producer with nineteen credits this is the most predictable money on the whole stack.

Up to 39.75% net on qualifying UK expenditure, for films with core production spend below £23.5 million. Above £15 million it tapers back towards the standard 25.5%. This is the strongest incentive this slate can reach, and it applies only to Kachhua, through the co-production with SunnyMarch.

SunnyMarch in London and A Team Productions in Belgium bring more than money. They bring access: their own national funds, regional schemes and broadcaster relationships. A co-producer is often worth more than the figure they put on paper.
Signed co-production contracts and a financing plan that is already half covered. Apply without that and you waste the round.

Funds and foundations working on oceans, plastic and climate, plus companies with a credible programme in that area. This is the only money on the whole slate that comes from outside the film chain, and Kachhua is the only title that can reach it. These parties are not buying a return; they are buying reach — how many people will look at a beach differently because of this film.

The final gap, usually covered against unsold territories. Small in amount, decisive in effect: this is the part that determines whether the whole thing closes. Dutch family offices with a connection to film or to the subject are more realistic here than institutional parties.
